blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Look up at night. You will see stars. Lots and lots of stars. All of them live in one big family. The family is called a galaxy. Our galaxy is called the Milky Way. It looks like a soft white road across the sky. You live in it. The Earth is in it. The sun is in it. Every star you can see is in it too.

blocks.prompt: The Road Made of Milk
blocks.text: A galaxy is a huge group of stars. The stars are held together by gravity, the same pull that keeps you on the ground. Our galaxy is the Milky Way. It has more stars than you could count in your whole life. Long ago, people saw a white band in the night sky. They thought it looked like spilled milk. That is why we call it the Milky Way. Then Galileo pointed a telescope at it. The white band broke apart into stars. Thousands of stars. The band is our own galaxy, seen from the inside. We are looking through it, like standing in a forest and looking at the trees.

blocks.prompt: The Road Made of Stars
blocks.text: On a dark night, far from town lights, a pale band stretches across the sky. People have watched it for thousands of years. The Greeks thought it looked like a spill of milk, and their word for milk, gala, is where we get the word galaxy. We now know what the band really is. It is our own galaxy, the Milky Way, seen edge on from the inside. Imagine a plate made of stars, wide and flat, with a bulge in the middle. Earth sits out in the flat part, about halfway from the middle to the edge. When you look along the plate, you see so many stars that they blur into a glowing road. When you look up out of the plate, you see only a few. The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. Light is the fastest thing there is, and it still takes 100,000 years to cross our galaxy. Inside it are hundreds of billions of stars, and our sun is only one of them.

blocks.prompt: How We Mapped a Galaxy From the Inside
blocks.text: Here is a strange problem. Nobody has ever seen our galaxy from outside. Every picture of the Milky Way you have ever seen is a drawing or a model, not a photograph. We are stuck inside it, and we cannot leave. So how do we know its shape? Astronomers worked it out the way you might map a forest you were standing in. They counted stars in every direction. They measured how far away those stars were, and how fast they were moving. Slowly, a shape emerged. The Milky Way is a barred spiral. It has a fat bulge at the middle, a straight bar of stars running through that bulge, and long curved arms wrapping around it like cream stirred into coffee. Our sun sits in a smaller arm called the Orion Arm, roughly 26,000 light-years from the center. That is a quiet suburb, far from the crowded downtown. At the very middle sits a black hole called Sagittarius A star. It weighs about four million times as much as our sun. Everything in the galaxy circles it, including us. The sun drags Earth around that center at about 800,000 kilometers per hour, and one full lap takes roughly 230 million years. The last time our solar system passed through this exact spot, the first dinosaurs were only just appearing.

blocks.prompt: The Great Debate
blocks.text: For most of human history, the Milky Way was the universe. Everything anyone had ever seen appeared to sit inside it. There was one puzzle. Scattered among the stars were faint smudges of light that astronomers called spiral nebulae. Nobody could agree what they were. Some argued they were clouds of glowing gas inside our own galaxy. Others argued something far bolder: that each smudge was an entire galaxy of its own, so distant that its billions of stars blurred into a single dim patch. In 1920 the two sides met in Washington for a public argument now known as the Great Debate. Neither side could win, because nobody knew how far away the smudges were. Distance was the whole question, and a woman named Henrietta Leavitt had already supplied the answer, though she did not live to see it used. Leavitt studied a type of star that brightens and dims on a regular beat. She found that the slower the beat, the brighter the star truly is. Find one of those stars, time its beat, compare its true brightness to how faint it looks from here, and you can calculate its distance. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found exactly such a star inside the Andromeda smudge. He timed it. The math gave an answer so large that the argument ended almost overnight. Andromeda was not a cloud in our galaxy. It was another galaxy, far outside our own, and the universe had just become unimaginably bigger than anyone had allowed. We now think the observable universe holds hundreds of billions of galaxies, and perhaps as many as two trillion. Andromeda is our nearest large neighbor, about 2.5 million light-years away, and it is also the most distant thing your naked eye can see. On a dark night it is a faint oval, and the light entering your eye left it 2.5 million years ago, long before your species existed. Andromeda is also coming toward us at about 110 kilometers every second. In roughly four billion years the two galaxies will meet and merge. That sounds like a catastrophe, but stars are so tiny compared to the gulfs between them that almost none will collide. The two galaxies will drift through each other like two swarms of gnats, and then settle into one.

6.title: The Galaxy We Live Inside
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Galaxias: Greek for milky, from gala
Galileo resolved the band into stars in 1610
Shapley versus Curtis, the Great Debate of 1920
Vera Rubin's rotation curves pointed to dark matter
Dark matter outweighs visible matter roughly five to one
Andromeda is closing at about 110 kilometers per second

blocks.prompt: The Galaxy You Cannot Step Outside Of
blocks.text: You live inside the thing you are trying to study. That is the central difficulty of galactic astronomy, and no telescope will ever fix it. We cannot walk outside the Milky Way and photograph it. Every image of our galaxy is a reconstruction, assembled from measurements taken at a single fixed point beside one unremarkable star. Astronomers are cartographers who cannot leave the forest. Start with what a galaxy is. It is not simply a lot of stars. It is a gravitationally bound system of stars, gas, dust, and something else we will come back to, all orbiting a common center. The Milky Way holds somewhere between one hundred and four hundred billion stars and spans roughly 100,000 light-years. Our sun lies about 26,000 light-years out in a minor spiral arm, circling the center once every 230 million years. At the middle crouches Sagittarius A star, a black hole with the mass of four million suns. The Greeks named the pale band overhead galaxias, from gala, milk. Galileo turned his telescope on it in 1610 and the milk shattered into individual stars. That single observation reframed the sky. The band was not a substance. It was a direction. We were looking edge on through the flat disk of our own galaxy, and the glow was the pile of stars stacked along the longest possible line of sight. Knowing our galaxy's shape did not tell us whether it was the whole universe. Faint spiral smudges dotted the sky, and in 1920 two astronomers argued the question in public. Harlow Shapley said the smudges were nearby gas clouds and the Milky Way was everything. Heber Curtis said each smudge was a separate island of stars. The debate settled nothing, because distance was unmeasured and every other argument was decoration. The measurement came from work by Henrietta Leavitt, who found that a certain kind of pulsing star beats more slowly the brighter it truly is. That relationship converts a flicker into a ruler. In 1923 Edwin Hubble found one of those stars in the Andromeda smudge, timed it, and calculated a distance no cloud inside our galaxy could possibly have. Curtis was right. Andromeda was a galaxy, and ours was one among many. Today the count of galaxies in the observable universe runs to hundreds of billions. Now the something else. In the 1970s Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit at different distances from a galaxy's center. Physics made a clear prediction: outer stars, feeling less gravity, should move more slowly, the way Neptune crawls while Mercury races. Rubin found the opposite. Stars at the outer edge moved about as fast as those near the middle. Either gravity behaves differently at galactic scale, or those galaxies contain far more mass than we can see, spread through a vast invisible halo. That unseen mass is called dark matter, and by the best current accounting it outweighs everything luminous in a galaxy by roughly five to one. The stars, which are all we can actually observe, may be a minority feature of the object we named after them. One more thing is worth sitting with. Andromeda is falling toward us at about 110 kilometers per second, and in roughly four billion years the two galaxies will collide. Almost no stars will strike each other. Stars are so small relative to the gulfs between them that the two systems will slide through one another, gravity will scramble the spiral arms, and eventually a single larger galaxy will settle out of the wreckage. Nothing will crash. Everything will change.
